claims.text: Severe plastic deformation will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys relative to conventional processing.
Severe plastic deformation will improve the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
The phosphorus-containing alloy before intervention is conventionally processed and predominantly crystalline.
Swaging followed by dynamic shear is a suitable severe-plastic-deformation route for inducing amorphization in a high-entropy alloy.
Room-temperature processing minimizes recovery during severe plastic deformation.
High-rate, low-temperature deformation can introduce a high density of dislocations, stacking faults, and twins.
Keeping the processing temperature sufficiently low prevents significant thermal recrystallization during deformation.
Alloys lacking sufficient inherent atomic disorder will respond less effectively to severe plastic deformation.
Severe plastic deformation creates a markedly increased defect density that can reorganize into local amorphous zones.
Coordinated stacking-fault and twin formation produces highly deformed regions that generate amorphous material upon reaching a critical defect concentration.
Severe plastic deformation increases atomic disorder and defect density.
The deformation-induced disorder lowers the nucleation barrier for amorphization.
Mechanically introduced disorder inhibits crystallization during subsequent thermal exposure.
Severely deformed samples will have a higher amorphous fraction than conventionally cooled or mildly deformed samples.
Severely deformed samples will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline samples.
Stabilization of the amorphous phase may improve mechanical properties.
Conventionally processed phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys have lower amorphous content than severely deformed counterparts.
Conventionally processed phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys have lower amorphous-state thermal stability than severely deformed counterparts.
High processing temperatures can compromise the intervention by permitting recovery and recrystallization.
